description: Heath, the miners, the three-day week, the Winter of Discontent, and Thatcher's 1979 election victory.
content_html:
Economic Crisis and Industrial Conflict

The affluence of the late 1950s and 1960s gave way in the 1970s to a period of severe economic difficulty. Britain faced a toxic combination of rising stagflation — simultaneously rising prices and rising unemployment — an industrial relations crisis, and the shock of rapidly rising oil prices. The 1973 OPEC oil embargo, following the Arab-Israeli war, quadrupled oil prices almost overnight. For an oil-importing economy like Britain, this was devastating.

Under both Heath (Conservative, 1970–1974) and Callaghan (Labour, 1976–1979), governments tried and failed to control wage rises, reduce inflation, and maintain industrial peace. Trade union power was at its peak. Britain’s unions had three million members in coal, steel, transport, and the public sector, and were willing to use strikes to pursue wage demands that governments believed were inflationary.

Key Fact

The three-day week was introduced on 1 January 1974. Edward Heath’s government ordered that commercial and industrial electricity use be limited to three days per week to conserve coal stocks during the miners’ strike. Television broadcasts ended at 10:30 pm. Offices worked by candlelight. The measure was a dramatic symbol of the state’s inability to keep modern Britain functioning in the face of industrial action.

Edward Heath and the Miners

Edward Heath came to power in June 1970 promising a more market-oriented approach to the economy. His government introduced the Industrial Relations Act 1971, designed to control union power through legal regulation of strikes. The unions refused to recognise the new Industrial Relations Court and the Act largely failed.

In January 1972, the National Union of Mineworkers (NUM) called its first national strike since 1926. Miners picketed power stations to prevent coal deliveries. At Saltley coke depot in Birmingham, mass picketing by thousands of workers (the “Battle of Saltley Gate”) forced police to close the gates. The government capitulated: the Wilberforce Report recommended pay rises of up to 20%. The miners’ victory showed that determined industrial action could defeat a government.

In late 1973, the NUM imposed an overtime ban, followed by an all-out strike in February 1974. Combined with the OPEC oil shock, this created an energy crisis so severe that Heath introduced the three-day week. Heath called a general election for February 1974 on the question “Who governs Britain?” — expecting public support. The result was inconclusive: the Conservatives won more votes but Labour won more seats. Harold Wilson formed a minority government. Heath had gambled and lost.

A second general election in October 1974 gave Labour a small working majority. Heath’s experiment in confronting the unions had ended in defeat. The episode became a defining reference point: throughout the 1970s, trade union power was seen by many Conservatives as the central problem facing Britain.

The Wilson and Callaghan Governments, 1974–1979

Harold Wilson’s Labour government (1974–1976) tried to manage industrial relations through the “Social Contract” — a voluntary agreement with the unions to moderate wage demands in exchange for social policies favourable to workers. Inflation reached 25% in 1975, one of the highest rates in post-war British history. Wilson resigned unexpectedly in March 1976 and was succeeded by James Callaghan.

Callaghan’s government faced an immediate financial crisis. By September 1976, the pound had fallen sharply and the government was forced to seek a loan from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), accepting harsh conditions — including public spending cuts — to secure it. This was a national humiliation and shook confidence in Labour’s economic management. Callaghan told the Labour Party Conference in September 1976 that governments could no longer spend their way out of recession — a significant break with post-war Keynesian orthodoxy.

Key Fact

The Winter of Discontent (1978–79) began when Callaghan’s government tried to hold pay rises to 5%. Lorry drivers, gravediggers, and refuse collectors went on strike. Bodies lay unburied in some areas. Mountains of rubbish piled up in parks and squares. The press gave the strikes devastating coverage. The Sun headline “Crisis? What crisis?” (attributed, possibly inaccurately, to Callaghan) summed up public contempt for the government’s response.

The 1979 General Election and Thatcher’s Victory

On 28 March 1979, a motion of no confidence in the Callaghan government passed by one vote — the first time a British government had fallen on such a vote since 1924. A general election was called for 3 May 1979. The Conservatives, now led by Margaret Thatcher, ran on a platform promising to control inflation, reduce union power, cut taxes, and reduce government spending. Their campaign used the slogan “Labour isn’t working” alongside an image of a long unemployment queue.

Thatcher won a majority of 43 seats. Her victory marked the end of the political era covered in this unit and the beginning of a new chapter in British political history. The post-war consensus — acceptance of the welfare state, mixed economy, and a degree of trade union power — that had underpinned British politics since 1945 was about to be challenged fundamentally.

Underlying the immediate crises was a deeper problem of industrial decline. British manufacturing — steel, shipbuilding, textiles, and cars — was losing competitiveness to West Germany, Japan, and other economies that had modernised more rapidly. British Leyland, the nationalised car manufacturer, was particularly troubled, with poor industrial relations, outdated models, and low productivity. The British car industry’s share of both domestic and export markets fell consistently through the 1970s.

Unemployment, which had been under 3% for most of the post-war period, reached over 1.5 million by the end of the 1970s. Long-term structural unemployment in former industrial regions — South Wales, the north-east of England, Clydeside in Scotland — was becoming visible. The optimism of Macmillan’s “never had it so good” years seemed a distant memory.
exam_tip_html: Economic history requires specific factual knowledge. For ‘8 marks — Explain Significance’ questions about the 1970s, make sure you distinguish between significance at the time (e.g. the three-day week caused immediate disruption and political damage to Heath) and over time (e.g. it became part of the Thatcherite narrative that unions had made Britain ungovernable). For ‘16 marks — Period Essay’ questions about who was responsible for Britain’s economic problems, avoid blaming only one factor: the OPEC oil shock (external), long-term industrial decline (structural), and trade union wage demands (internal) all played a part. The strongest answers weigh these factors against each other.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 1970s saw Britain hit by stagflation, the 1973 oil shock, and intense industrial conflict. Heath introduced the three-day week (January 1974) after the miners’ strike; he then lost the February 1974 election after asking “Who governs Britain?”
  • The Winter of Discontent (1978–79) — strikes by lorry drivers, gravediggers, and refuse collectors — gave a devastating impression of national breakdown, directly causing Labour’s defeat in the May 1979 election.
  • Margaret Thatcher’s victory in May 1979, on a platform of controlling inflation and reducing union power, ended the post-war consensus era and opened a new chapter in British political history.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the three-day week introduced in January 1974.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- Commercial and industrial electricity use was limited to three days per week to conserve coal stocks during the miners' strike; offices worked by candlelight and television broadcasts ended at 10:30 pm.
- The measure was introduced by Edward Heath on 1 January 1974 and was seen as a dramatic demonstration of the government's inability to manage the energy crisis caused by industrial action.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Winter of Discontent in 1978–1979.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple cause identified, limited explanation.
Secure: Clear cause with explanation and factual support.
Mastering: Detailed explanation, precise evidence, chain of causation clear.

Causes may include:
- Callaghan's government attempted to hold pay rises to 5%, well below inflation; unions whose members' real wages were falling refused to accept this cap.
- Long-term frustration with wage restraint after years of economic crisis; unions had cooperated with the Social Contract but felt Labour had failed to deliver.
- The OPEC oil shock and inflation had eroded living standards through the mid-1970s, making workers determined to claw back purchasing power.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Edward Heath's decision to call a general election in February 1974 on the question 'Who governs Britain?'
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple consequence, limited development.
Secure: Clear consequence with explanation and evidence.
Mastering: Detailed consequence, precise evidence, wider significance addressed.

Consequences may include:
- Labour won more seats than the Conservatives despite fewer votes; Heath was unable to form a government and Wilson returned to power — demonstrating that Heath's gamble had failed.
- Heath was later replaced as Conservative leader by Thatcher in 1975, who drew the lesson that the unions must be confronted and defeated, not negotiated with.
- The election result was seen as demonstrating trade union power: the miners had, in effect, determined the outcome of a general election.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant was the 1973 OPEC oil embargo in causing Britain's economic problems in the 1970s? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple points, limited evidence.
Developing: Some significance explained, basic evidence.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time addressed, evidence well-chosen.
Mastering: Sophisticated analysis, precise evidence, sustained argument weighing OPEC against other factors.

At the time: quadrupled oil prices overnight; combined with miners' strike to create energy crisis requiring three-day week; contributed to stagflation and 25% inflation in 1975.
Limits: long-term industrial decline pre-dated OPEC; trade union power was a domestic factor; the oil shock affected all Western economies but Britain's response was uniquely disruptive.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The trade unions were the main cause of Britain's political and economic problems in the 1970s.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement, little evidence.
Developing: Some evaluation, limited range of evidence.
Secure: Clear evaluation, agreement and disagreement addressed, factual knowledge used.
Mastering: Sophisticated evaluation, precise evidence, substantiated overall judgement.

Agreement: miners' strikes (1972, 1974) brought down the Heath government; the Winter of Discontent ended the Callaghan government; industrial disputes in manufacturing damaged productivity and competitiveness.

Disagreement: external factors (OPEC oil shock 1973) caused immediate crisis; long-term industrial decline (failing car, steel, shipbuilding industries) was structural; government mismanagement (IMF crisis 1976) also played a role; union militancy was partly a response to falling real wages caused by inflation.

[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Margaret Thatcher's 1979 general election campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- The Conservative campaign used the slogan 'Labour isn't working' alongside an image of a long unemployment queue, directly attacking Labour's economic management.
- Thatcher promised to control inflation, reduce trade union power, cut taxes, and reduce government spending — a platform presenting a clear break from the post-war consensus.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

flashcard_questions.q: When was the three-day week introduced and who introduced it?
flashcard_questions.a: 1 January 1974 by Edward Heath's Conservative government.

flashcard_questions.q: What question did Heath ask in the February 1974 election?
flashcard_questions.a: 'Who governs Britain?' — he lost and Wilson returned to power.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Winter of Discontent?
What was the Winter of Discontent?
flashcard_questions.a: Widespread public sector strikes (lorry drivers, gravediggers, refuse collectors) that caused national disruption.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to the Callaghan government on 28 March 1979?
flashcard_questions.a: It lost a vote of no confidence by one vote — the first government to fall this way since 1924.
Rising inflation combined with rising unemployment — previously thought impossible by conventional economics.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the outcome of the 1972 miners' strike?
flashcard_questions.a: The government capitulated; the Wilberforce Report recommended pay rises of up to 20% — a major union victory.

flashcard_questions.q: What percentage rate did UK inflation reach in 1975?
flashcard_questions.a: Approximately 25% — one of the highest in post-war British history.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did Heath's Industrial Relations Act 1971 fail?
flashcard_questions.a: Unions refused to recognise the Industrial Relations Court; the Act could not be enforced effectively.

flashcard_questions.q: What slogan did the Conservatives use in the 1979 election?
What was the Social Contract under Wilson's 1974 government?
flashcard_questions.a: A voluntary agreement with unions to moderate wage demands in exchange for favourable social policies.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the significance of Margaret Thatcher's victory in May 1979?
flashcard_questions.a: Britain's first female PM; ended the post-war consensus era and began a new era of market-oriented economics.

glossary_terms.definition: A period of high inflation combined with high unemployment and stagnant economic growth — a combination that conventional economic theory had predicted was impossible.
An emergency measure introduced by Heath's government in January 1974, limiting commercial and industrial electricity use to three days per week to conserve coal stocks during the miners' strike.
Conservative Prime Minister 1970–1974, whose government was brought down partly by the miners' strikes of 1972 and 1974.
Labour Prime Minister 1976–1979, who faced a severe economic crisis including IMF intervention in 1976 and the Winter of Discontent in 1978–79.

The period from late 1978 to early 1979 when widespread strikes by public sector workers — dustmen, gravediggers, lorry drivers, and hospital workers — created dramatic disruption and images that damaged the Labour government irreparably.
Conservative Party leader who won the 1979 general election, becoming Britain's first female Prime Minister; associated with the dismantling of the post-war consensus.
